paras: The vigilante hangings near Reynosa were the killings in December 1881 of three men described as 'noted bandits' and of a fourth man, Zefarino Mercado, by Mexican vigilants who called themselves a 'Commission', in Mexico near and south of Reynosa. The news reached American papers through dispatches from Brownsville, Texas, and some later briefs placed the hangings in Brownsville itself.

The dispatches set the hangings amid other violence between Reynosa and Camargo, including the reported murder of a young man named Cavazos, his bride and her mother by bandits, and a fight between smugglers and customs guards near Ceja ranch.

According to a Brownsville dispatch of December 21, three noted bandits, two of them known by the same name, Manuel Asundo, and the third as Lucas Franco, were captured near Reynosa 'yesterday' and hanged by Mexican vigilants. Another version of the dispatch said they were hanged on Wednesday, and one placed the hanging about forty miles south of Reynosa.

A second Brownsville roundup, dated December 22, added that Zefarino Mercado had also been hung by vigilants south of Reynosa. Citing advices from Edinburg, one paper described Mercado as 'one of the Bishop murderers' and said he had been hanged by a Commission.
No report of arrests, an inquiry or any official response on either side of the border appears in the coverage.

White papers from Maine to Tennessee printed the Brownsville dispatch as a few lines under headlines such as 'Mexican Bandits Lynched' and 'Three Noted Bandits Hanged', calling the dead 'noted bandits' without comment. The Wheeling Register grouped the hangings with murders and a smugglers' fight under the headline 'Hanging, Murdering and Marauding on the Frontier'.

Weeks later, the South Kentuckian of Hopkinsville condensed the items into one-line notes that 'Three Mexican bandits were lynched at Brownsville, Texas' and that 'Salferno Marcade' was hung by vigilants there, moving both hangings from Mexico to the dispatch dateline.

Most versions counted three bandits hanged together, but the Wheeling Register named only two, Manual Asunas and Lucas Franco. The place also varied, from 'near Renosa' and 'at Reynosa' to about forty miles south of it; the Brownsville location in the Kentucky briefs is better read as the dateline of the original dispatches.

reader.title: Vigilante hangings near Reynosa, Mexico (1881)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Bands of Mexican vigilants calling themselves a 'Commission' captured and hanged men described as bandits, and in one case a man accused as one of 'the Bishop murderers', in Mexico near and south of Reynosa (A1, A3, A4).

The men were hanged by 'vigilants' and the Portland headline called it a lynching, on the ground that they were 'noted bandits' or, in Mercado's case, one of 'the Bishop murderers' (A1, A3, A4); the dispatches call the killers a 'band' and a 'Commission' but give no number, and no paper describes the Commission's authority (A3, A4).

Every version traces to dispatches dated at Brownsville, Texas, on Dec. 21-22, 1881 (A1, A2, A3, A4, A5), and the later South Kentuckian briefs condense the same items (A7, A8); no local Mexican or border report or follow-up was found.

framing.detail: Papers ran the Brownsville dispatch as a few lines under 'Mexican Bandits Lynched' or 'Three Noted Bandits Hanged', calling the dead 'noted bandits' without comment.
The Wheeling Register grouped the hangings with a murdered family and a smugglers' fight under 'Hanging, Murdering and Marauding on the Frontier'.
The South Kentuckian reduced each item to a single line among other killings and accidents in its General News column.
